description: Cache mapping, replacement, write policies, locality and performance.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of cache memory?
questions.optionA: Reduce average memory access time
questions.explanation: Cache keeps frequently used information closer to the CPU.

questions.questionText: What is a cache line?
questions.optionA: A block of data stored in cache
questions.explanation: A cache line is a unit of data transferred and stored in cache.

questions.questionText: What is direct-mapped cache?
questions.optionA: Each memory block maps to exactly one cache line
questions.explanation: In direct mapping, each memory block has exactly one possible cache location.

questions.questionText: What is fully associative cache?
questions.optionA: A block can be placed in any cache line
questions.optionB: A block has only one fixed line
questions.explanation: Fully associative mapping allows a memory block to occupy any cache line.

questions.questionText: What is set-associative cache?
questions.optionA: A block maps to a set and can occupy one line within that set
questions.optionB: A block maps to every line
questions.optionC: A block has only one global location
questions.explanation: Set-associative cache combines fixed set mapping with multiple choices inside the set.

questions.questionText: What is a cache tag used for?
questions.optionA: Identifying which memory block is stored
questions.explanation: The tag identifies the memory block associated with a cache entry.

questions.questionText: What is a valid bit?
questions.optionA: Indicates whether a cache entry contains valid data
questions.explanation: The valid bit tells whether the cache entry is valid.

questions.questionText: What is a dirty bit?
questions.optionA: Indicates modified cache data that may need write-back
questions.explanation: A dirty bit is used in write-back caches to identify modified data.

questions.questionText: What is write-through cache?
questions.optionA: Writes are propagated to lower-level memory immediately
questions.optionB: Writes remain only in cache forever
questions.explanation: Write-through updates lower-level memory as writes occur.

questions.questionText: What is write-back cache?
questions.optionA: Modified data is written to lower memory when the cache block is replaced
questions.explanation: Write-back delays lower-memory updates until a modified block is evicted.

questions.questionText: What is a cache hit ratio of 90%?
questions.optionA: 90% of accesses are cache hits
questions.explanation: A 90% hit ratio means 90 out of every 100 accesses hit in cache on average.

questions.questionText: What is miss penalty?
questions.optionA: Extra time required when a cache miss occurs
questions.explanation: Miss penalty is the additional time needed to obtain data after a cache miss.

questions.questionText: Which replacement policy removes the least recently used block?
questions.optionA: LRU
questions.explanation: LRU stands for Least Recently Used.

questions.questionText: What does FIFO replacement remove first?
questions.optionA: The block that entered the cache first
questions.explanation: FIFO removes the oldest cache entry first.

questions.questionText: What is the AMAT formula commonly used for a simple cache?
questions.optionA: Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty
questions.explanation: Average Memory Access Time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.

questions.questionText: If hit ratio increases, what generally happens to average memory access time?
questions.optionA: It decreases
questions.optionD: It is unaffected in every case
questions.explanation: A higher hit ratio generally reduces the frequency of expensive cache misses.

questions.questionText: What is compulsory miss?
questions.optionA: A miss caused because a block is accessed for the first time
questions.optionB: A miss caused only by a full cache
questions.explanation: A compulsory miss occurs on the first reference to a block.

questions.questionText: What is capacity miss?
questions.optionA: A miss caused when the cache cannot hold the required working set
questions.explanation: Capacity misses occur because the cache is too small for the working set.

questions.questionText: What is conflict miss?
questions.optionA: A miss caused by multiple blocks competing for the same cache location or set
questions.explanation: Conflict misses result from mapping restrictions.

questions.questionText: Which mapping is simplest to implement?
questions.optionA: Direct mapping
questions.explanation: Direct mapping is simple because each block has one possible cache location.

questions.questionText: Which cache mapping provides the most placement flexibility?
questions.optionA: Fully associative
questions.explanation: Fully associative mapping allows a block to occupy any cache line.

questions.questionText: What is a cache block offset used for?
questions.optionA: Selecting a byte or word within a cache block
questions.explanation: The block offset identifies a particular byte or word inside a cache block.

questions.questionText: What does the index field identify in a set-associative cache?
questions.optionA: The cache set
questions.explanation: The index identifies the cache set.

questions.questionText: What does locality help cache performance?
questions.optionA: It makes recently or nearby accessed data likely to be reused
questions.explanation: Temporal and spatial locality allow cache to exploit likely future accesses.

questions.questionText: Which cache level is generally closest to the CPU core?
questions.optionA: L1 cache
questions.explanation: L1 cache is generally the smallest and fastest cache closest to the core.
